title: Posy and the Smoky Phoenix
markdown:
In a field so green it might have been spilled from a giant’s paint, lived Posy, a tidy piglet whose favorite place in the world was her mud puddle. Not any puddle. Hers: edges just so, no stray twigs, bumpy bits smoothed with her snout. Every morning she woke, wiggled her pink nose until it seemed it might wiggle off (it never did), and trotted. Trot, trot, trot. She splashed just so, little trotters making perfect ripples, not a splish out of place.

Every day was the same, and she liked the same: wake, wiggle, zoom to the puddle, edges just right. She smoothed the mud. She splashed carefully so the water would not go too high. Doing things just right was her talent. And then she’d splash alone. Sometimes, when sunbeams danced on dew and dandelions whispered to the breeze, she sighed a tiny piggy sigh. She wished for someone to splash with. Someone to share the happy squelches. The puddle was a lonely kind of perfect.

Until a puff of smoke smelling of warm cinnamon cookies drifted down and landed beside the puddle with a soft plink. After it, with another little poof, tumbled a tiny fluffy creature like a marshmallow that had learned wings. Big curious eyes blinked.

Oh, squeaked Posy, snout twitching. Hello, little fluffy thing.

The creature wiggled fuzzy wings until they shimmered like small rainbows, then sneezed a tiny sneeze. Another puff of cinnamon smoke tickled Posy’s nose. She giggled. A fizzy tickle went through her whole body.

Who are you, she asked, trying to sound brave while her knees jigged.

The creature chirped like tiny bells. Ember. A phoenix. First rebirth went a little smoky. A hiccup, and another cinnamon puff from her beak.

A smoky phoenix. Posy’s eyes went round. She had only heard stories. A smoky one was new.

Every day Ember tried to fly. She’d flap, ready for soaring, and every little flutter sent a cheerful cookie-scented puff. If she watched a butterfly: poof. If a friendly ladybug surprised her: poof, poof. It was as if a tiny warm cloud of baking followed her everywhere, even to the puddle’s neat rim, which Posy had just smoothed.

Posy giggled until she hiccupped. Every sneeze, every flap, every wiggle of Ember’s tail made cinnamon magic. Smoke tickled her nose, then her ears, then her curly tail. Being the tidy piglet she was, she tried to help. She fanned with her trotters and more smoke billowed, warm as an oven door. She tried to catch it in her snout, which is like catching a whisper on a windy day. The puddle’s edges wobbled. A cinnamon ring landed on the mud like a donut nobody had asked for.

Then she noticed, in a pause as still as grass. The smoke was not really mess. It smelled of happy holidays and warm hugs and a kitchen where someone was kind. Ember wasn’t clumsy. Ember was Ember: a marshmallow bird with a cinnamon sneeze and a heart full of sun.

Posy looked at her perfectly tidy puddle, then at Ember blowing smoke rings like little cinnamon donuts. She took a brave piggy breath.

You know what, Ember. You’re not messy. You’re sparkly. Like a walking cinnamon bun. Ember’s eyes shone.

Posy did something braver still. She nudged Ember toward a sunny patch of soft dry grass. Maybe you’d be more comfortable here. Not a mud puddle. Warm. Cozy.

Ember nestled in. The grass felt as soft as a cloud. Cinnamon smoke settled around her like a gentle fragrant blanket. A tiny puff, smelling of warm cinnamon and happiness, floated toward Posy. She closed her eyes and breathed it in: the warmth of the grass, the sweet spice, the gentle shimmer of Ember’s wings. They sat without rushing. Then Posy carefully dipped her snout into the very edge of her puddle and brought a tiny perfect wonderfully muddy kiss to Ember’s fuzzy head. Ember chirped with delight. A spark of warm gold pulsed from her little phoenix chest. Not only a tidy puddle. Not only a smoky friend. The beginning of something special.

They became the best of friends. Muddy splashes and cinnamon puffs mixed until the field felt like a hug. Posy’s puddle stayed fairly tidy, because she liked it that way. It was also the coziest, happiest, most cinnamon-scented puddle for miles. On extra-warm days, when the dandelions were extra fluffy, you could hear giggles, squelches, and the gentle poof of smoke, and nobody asked the puddle to be lonelier than it needed to be.
